text: Lancet 2007; 369: 1090–8. Correction. ibid.; 370: 220. 19. Hooper L, et al. Omega 3 fatty acids for prevention and treat- ment of cardiovascular disease. Available in The Cochrane Da- tabase of Systematic Reviews; Issue 4. Chichester: John Wiley; 2004 (accessed 30/05/08). Inflammatory and auto-immune disorders. Omega-3 fat- ty acids have effects on several immunological and inflammato- ry mediators1,2 and have been tried in a number of inflammatory and auto-immune disorders. Beneficial effects have been report- ed in rheumatoid arthritis3 (p.11) and in glomerular kidney disease4-6 (p.1504), but results in kidney transplantation (p.1813) have been mixed, and systematic reviews7,8 suggest no signifi- cant effect on rejection episodes or graft survival. Some studies have shown benefit in psoriasis (p.1583), both with oral9,10 and with intravenous dosage,11,12 but other studies found neither the oral13 nor the topical14 route to be effective. Variable benefit has been seen in inflammatory bowel disease15 (p.1697) although this may relate to the different formulations used. In Crohn’s dis- ease, a systematic review found that enteric-coated formulations helped to maintain remission,16 but a subsequent randomised study using a gelatin capsule formulation found no benefit.17 Similarly, a systematic review found that conventional formula- tions were not of benefit in patients with ulcerative colitis.18 Fish oils have also been tried in lung disorders, although systematic reviews have found little evidence of benefit in asthma;19,20 in cystic fibrosis, limited benefit has been reported,21 with one study22 reporting that fish oil supplementation reduced the need for antibacterial treatment. Preliminary evidence23 also suggests that omega-3 supplementation may reduce inflammatory mark- ers and improve dyspnoea in chronic obstructive pulmonary dis- ease. 1. Simopoulos AP.
